flashcard_questions.a: When a business expands from within, without merging with or taking over another business.
When a business grows by merging with or taking over another company.
When two businesses combine to form one new company.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a takeover of a company?
flashcard_questions.a: When one business buys more than 50% of the shares in another.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes a takeover hostile rather than friendly?
flashcard_questions.a: The target company's management opposes the deal.
A country experiencing rapid economic growth and industrialisation.
The cost advantages of growing larger that reduce the average cost per unit.

flashcard_questions.q: Which grocery business uses automated warehouse robots to pick and pack orders?
What brand did the 2009 merger of T-Mobile and Orange later become?
What price did Disney pay to take over Pixar in 2006?
What did Kraft do to the Somerdale factory after taking over Cadbury?
flashcard_questions.a: It closed the factory, making hundreds of workers redundant.

flashcard_questions.q: What proportion of all mergers fail?
What must a public limited company publish that its competitors can read?
What risk do the original owners of a plc face if shareholders gain a 51% majority?
flashcard_questions.a: They lose control of the company.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is retained profit a cheap source of finance for a growing business?
flashcard_questions.a: There is no interest to pay on it.

notes: 15 cards: 7 term→definition (organic, inorganic, merger, takeover, hostile, emerging market, economies of scale), 4 concept→named example (Ocado, EE, Disney/Pixar $7.4bn, Kraft/Somerdale), 3 single-fact disadvantage/advantage cards (80% of mergers fail, published accounts, 51% loss of control), 1 finance fact. Dropped the Tesco–Tata and RBS–NatWest examples to keep the deck at 15; four named deals already cover merger and takeover.
